theory.title: Audience adaptation and persuasive register
theory.explanation: Persuasion depends not only on what is argued but on how an argument meets the audience's knowledge, expectations, interests and relationship to the speaker. Audience adaptation is not a licence to distort evidence or flatter listeners. It involves selecting an appropriate register, explaining unfamiliar concepts, anticipating shared assumptions and making the practical relevance explicit. A specialist audience may expect technical terminology and methodological qualifications; a general audience may need the same reasoning anchored in concrete consequences. Register also shapes interpersonal distance: a formal institutional statement, a collegial briefing and a public appeal can communicate the same proposition while creating different relationships. Framing directs attention towards particular aspects of an issue, so it should be transparent about what it foregrounds and what it leaves outside the frame. At C2 level, adapt the route into a complex idea while preserving its evidential limits, and assess whether a rhetorical choice clarifies, engages or manipulates.
theory.tip: Change the explanation, examples and emphasis for the audience; do not change the evidential standard.

patterns.label: Establish audience knowledge
patterns.pattern: Define the terms the audience needs, not every term the speaker knows.
examples: For readers outside the field, the key distinction is between a forecast and a guarantee.

patterns.label: Translate technical relevance
patterns.pattern: Connect specialist concepts to decisions or consequences.
examples: In practical terms, the revised threshold determines which applications receive priority.

patterns.label: Choose a fitting register
patterns.pattern: Match formality and interpersonal distance to the setting.
examples: The briefing is deliberately measured; the public statement is more direct.

patterns.label: Frame transparently
patterns.pattern: State what aspect is foregrounded and acknowledge relevant limits.
examples: This comparison focuses on cost, although access and distribution also matter.

phrases.english: Correlation alone does not establish causation.
phrases.spanish: La correlación por sí sola no demuestra causalidad.

phrases.english: A third variable may account for the observed relationship.
phrases.spanish: Una tercera variable puede explicar la relación observada.

phrases.english: The proposed mechanism remains to be demonstrated.
phrases.spanish: El mecanismo propuesto aún debe demostrarse.

phrases.english: The pattern is consistent with, but does not prove, a causal effect.
phrases.spanish: El patrón es compatible con un efecto causal, pero no lo demuestra.
phrases.note: Calibra la fuerza de la conclusión.

grammar.english: The association may be attributable to an unmeasured confounder.
grammar.spanish: La asociación podría deberse a un factor de confusión no medido.
grammar.note: Usa may be attributable to para proponer una causa sin afirmarla.

grammar.english: Had the groups been comparable at baseline, the estimate would have been more reliable.
grammar.spanish: Si los grupos hubieran sido comparables al inicio, la estimación habría sido más fiable.
grammar.note: Inversión condicional formal para evaluar condiciones no cumplidas.

reading.english: A city introduces a congestion charge; traffic falls, but fuel prices rise at the same time.
reading.spanish: Una ciudad introduce una tasa de congestión; el tráfico baja, pero el combustible se encarece simultáneamente.
reading.note: Evalúa explicaciones concurrentes antes de atribuir el cambio a una sola medida.

writing.english: Although the intervention preceded the change, temporal order alone is insufficient to establish causation.
writing.spanish: Aunque la intervención precedió al cambio, el orden temporal por sí solo no basta para demostrar causalidad.
writing.note: Concede una observación válida y limita la inferencia.

speaking.english: Which competing explanation would you investigate first, and why?
speaking.spanish: ¿Qué explicación alternativa investigarías primero y por qué?
speaking.prompt: Compare two plausible causal explanations and justify which evidence would distinguish them.
speaking.promptSpanish: Compara dos explicaciones causales plausibles y justifica qué pruebas permitirían distinguirlas.

listening.english: The apparent effect diminished once the researchers adjusted for baseline differences.
listening.spanish: El efecto aparente disminuyó cuando los investigadores ajustaron las diferencias iniciales.
listening.note: Escucha cómo el ajuste estadístico modifica una interpretación causal.

examples.english: The programme coincided with a decline in absences, but staffing levels changed too.
examples.spanish: El programa coincidió con una reducción de ausencias, pero también cambió la plantilla.
examples.note: La coincidencia temporal deja abierta una explicación alternativa.

communication.english: I would be reluctant to infer causation until reverse causality had been ruled out.
communication.spanish: Sería prudente no inferir causalidad hasta descartar la causalidad inversa.
communication.note: Expresa cautela metodológica sin descartar la hipótesis.

phrases.english: For an audience unfamiliar with the technical detail...
phrases.spanish: Para un público que no conoce los detalles técnicos...

phrases.english: The point can be put more plainly without losing precision.
phrases.spanish: La idea puede expresarse con más sencillez sin perder precisión.
phrases.note: Simplifica la forma sin sacrificar contenido.

phrases.english: That framing is likely to resonate with stakeholders who...
phrases.spanish: Ese encuadre probablemente conecte con las partes interesadas que...
phrases.note: Relaciona el encuadre con intereses del público.

phrases.english: The choice of register subtly shifts the relationship with the reader.
phrases.spanish: La elección del registro modifica sutilmente la relación con el lector.
phrases.note: Explica el efecto interpersonal del registro.

grammar.english: Were the audience less familiar with the field, I would define the term before using it.
grammar.spanish: Si el público conociera menos el campo, definiría el término antes de usarlo.
grammar.note: Inversión condicional formal para adaptar el discurso a conocimiento hipotético.

grammar.english: Not so much the evidence as its presentation determines whether the point is accessible.
grammar.spanish: No tanto la evidencia como su presentación determina si la idea resulta accesible.
grammar.note: Estructura contrastiva para distinguir contenido y presentación.

reading.english: Effective adaptation changes the route into an idea, not the integrity of the idea itself.
reading.spanish: Una adaptación eficaz cambia el camino hacia una idea, no la integridad de la idea misma.

writing.english: Although the terminology is necessarily specialised, the practical implication can be stated in accessible terms.
writing.spanish: Aunque la terminología sea necesariamente especializada, la implicación práctica puede expresarse de forma accesible.
writing.note: Conserva precisión técnica y traduce su relevancia.

speaking.english: How would you explain the same policy to specialists and to the general public?
speaking.spanish: ¿Cómo explicarías la misma política a especialistas y al público general?
speaking.prompt: Adapt one complex argument for two contrasting audiences, explaining the changes in register, framing and assumed knowledge.
speaking.promptSpanish: Adapta un argumento complejo a dos públicos distintos y explica los cambios de registro, encuadre y conocimiento supuesto.

listening.english: The presenter retained the evidence but changed the framing to address the audience's priorities.
listening.spanish: La ponente mantuvo la evidencia, pero cambió el encuadre para atender las prioridades del público.
listening.note: Reconoce adaptación retórica sin alterar la base probatoria.

examples.english: Rather than referring to a fiscal externality, the speaker described the cost shifted onto local households.
examples.spanish: En lugar de hablar de una externalidad fiscal, la ponente describió el coste trasladado a los hogares locales.
examples.note: Traduce un concepto técnico a consecuencias reconocibles.

communication.english: The technical distinction matters here, but I will first outline why it affects the decision.
communication.spanish: La distinción técnica importa aquí, pero primero explicaré por qué afecta a la decisión.
communication.note: Orienta a un público no especializado hacia la relevancia.

items.prompt: A technical report is being presented to residents with no specialist background. What is the best adaptation?
options: Explain the key terms and connect the findings to decisions residents face.
Remove every qualification to make the message shorter.
Use more technical language to establish authority.
items.answer: Explain the key terms and connect the findings to decisions residents face.

items.prompt: Which change adapts register without changing the underlying evidence?
options: Replace unexplained jargon with a precise everyday explanation.
Omit results that complicate the message.
Present an uncertain estimate as a guarantee.
items.answer: Replace unexplained jargon with a precise everyday explanation.

items.prompt: A speaker wants to build rapport with a professional audience. What is most appropriate?
options: Acknowledge shared professional concerns while maintaining analytical precision.
Assume all listeners share the same political views.
Use personal flattery instead of evidence.
items.answer: Acknowledge shared professional concerns while maintaining analytical precision.

items.prompt: Which framing is most transparent?
options: This comparison focuses on cost; access and distributional effects are also relevant.
Only cost matters, and no other perspective is legitimate.
The figures speak for themselves without assumptions.
items.answer: This comparison focuses on cost; access and distributional effects are also relevant.

items.prompt: What is a pragmatic effect of shifting from “you must” to “you may wish to consider”?
options: It reduces directiveness and gives the addressee more room to decide.
It makes the proposition grammatically impossible.
It guarantees agreement.
items.answer: It reduces directiveness and gives the addressee more room to decide.

items.prompt: A public appeal uses a concrete household example. What should the speaker ensure?
options: That the example illustrates the broader evidence without being presented as proof by itself.
That one anecdote replaces population-level data.
That the example is emotionally vivid even if misleading.
items.answer: That the example illustrates the broader evidence without being presented as proof by itself.

items.prompt: Which audience needs the most explicit methodological qualification?
options: An audience making a high-stakes decision based on uncertain projections.
An audience that has already agreed with every claim.
An audience for whom accuracy is irrelevant.
items.answer: An audience making a high-stakes decision based on uncertain projections.

items.prompt: What is the main risk of over-adapting a message to please listeners?
options: The speaker may distort complexity or conceal evidence that challenges the audience's expectations.
The speaker may become too accurate.
The speaker may explain unfamiliar terms.
items.answer: The speaker may distort complexity or conceal evidence that challenges the audience's expectations.

items.prompt: Which opening best signals relevance to a non-specialist audience?
options: The decision affects how quickly local families can access the service.
This presentation concerns a multivariate optimisation framework.
The following terminology requires no explanation.
items.answer: The decision affects how quickly local families can access the service.

items.prompt: What should remain stable across different audience versions?
options: The core evidence, reasoning and honest statement of uncertainty.
The exact wording and technical density.
The emotional appeal, regardless of context.
items.answer: The core evidence, reasoning and honest statement of uncertainty.

items.prompt: Choose the most suitable register: “We would be grateful if you ___ your comments by Friday.”
options: could submit
submit you
will submitting
items.answer: could submit

items.prompt: Complete the inversion: “Only when the implications are clear ___ the audience assess the proposal.”
options: can
the audience can
does
items.answer: can

items.prompt: Choose the precise structure: “The findings are relevant not because they are dramatic, ___ because they affect access.”
options: but
rather than
although
items.answer: but

items.prompt: Select the appropriate hedge for a public briefing: “The estimate ___ indicate a gradual improvement.”
options: appears to
proves to
must
items.answer: appears to

items.prompt: Complete: “The point is easier to grasp when it is expressed ___ practical consequences.”
options: in terms of
by means
as
items.answer: in terms of

items.prompt: Choose the correct cleft sentence: “What matters most ___ how the change affects users.”
options: is
are
be
items.answer: is

items.prompt: Select the accurate concessive clause: “However familiar the terminology ___, the decision still needs explanation.”
options: may be
is being
be
items.answer: may be

items.prompt: Complete: “The briefing was tailored ___ the concerns of frontline staff.”
options: to
for
with
items.answer: to

items.prompt: Choose the correct correlative: “The message was neither simplistic ___ needlessly technical.”
options: nor
or
and
items.answer: nor

items.prompt: Select the most precise phrase: “The speaker made the technical distinction ___ to a wider audience.”
options: accessible
accessibility
access
items.answer: accessible

items.prompt: What did engineers primarily want from the briefing?
options: Technical assumptions, uncertainty ranges and model sensitivity.
Personal stories from residents only.
A guarantee that pollution would fall.
items.answer: Technical assumptions, uncertainty ranges and model sensitivity.

items.prompt: What were residents most concerned about?
options: Local exposure, timing of change and available safeguards.
The mathematical notation used in the model.
The institute's internal staffing structure.
items.answer: Local exposure, timing of change and available safeguards.

items.prompt: What remained shared between the two briefings?
options: The underlying analysis and its evidential basis.
The exact wording and technical density.
The same examples and level of detail.
items.answer: The underlying analysis and its evidential basis.

items.prompt: Why did the public version use maps and neighbourhood examples?
options: To make the possible local effects easier to interpret.
To conceal the uncertainty ranges.
To replace the model with anecdotes.
items.answer: To make the possible local effects easier to interpret.

items.prompt: What misconception did some staff initially hold?
options: That fewer equations necessarily meant less rigour.
That engineers wanted detailed assumptions.
That residents cared about local exposure.
items.answer: That fewer equations necessarily meant less rigour.

items.prompt: How did the public briefing make uncertainty visible?
options: It described projections as scenarios and identified their assumptions and limits.
It removed all qualifications.
It promised a particular outcome.
items.answer: It described projections as scenarios and identified their assumptions and limits.

items.prompt: Why was the public version not less rigorous according to the project lead?
options: It removed unhelpful detail while retaining and foregrounding relevant limitations.
It used more equations than the technical version.
It avoided mentioning uncertainty.
items.answer: It removed unhelpful detail while retaining and foregrounding relevant limitations.

items.prompt: What function did the technical briefing serve?
options: It enabled specialists to challenge inputs and test assumptions.
It persuaded residents to accept the proposal.
It guaranteed the model's accuracy.
items.answer: It enabled specialists to challenge inputs and test assumptions.

items.prompt: When does audience adaptation become misleading?
options: When presentation conceals a material difference in what the evidence supports.
When different groups receive different examples.
When technical terms are explained.
items.answer: When presentation conceals a material difference in what the evidence supports.

items.prompt: What is the central principle of the passage?
options: Adapt presentation to audience needs while preserving evidence and uncertainty.
Use one identical script for every audience.
Prioritise accessibility over factual accuracy.
items.answer: Adapt presentation to audience needs while preserving evidence and uncertainty.

content.passage:
A research institute was asked to explain a new air-quality model to two groups: municipal engineers and residents living near a proposed traffic corridor. The model estimated changes in pollution under several traffic-management scenarios. Engineers wanted to inspect assumptions, confidence intervals and the sensitivity of the projections. Residents, by contrast, were primarily concerned with where exposure might increase, how quickly changes could be noticed and what safeguards were available.

The institute prepared two briefings based on the same analysis. The technical version retained the modelling terminology and detailed uncertainty ranges. The public version used maps and neighbourhood examples to show how exposure might vary across streets. It explained that the projections were scenarios rather than promises and identified the assumptions on which the estimates depended.

Some staff initially worried that the public briefing was less rigorous because it contained fewer equations. The project lead disagreed. Removing detail that did not help residents interpret the decision was not the same as removing uncertainty. Indeed, the public version stated the limits more prominently and explained what further monitoring would be needed. The technical briefing, meanwhile, allowed specialists to challenge the model's inputs and test alternative assumptions.

The two versions were not identical, nor should they have been. Their credibility depended on a shared evidential basis, clear disclosure of uncertainty and a form suited to the decisions each audience needed to make. Adaptation became misleading only where a difference in presentation concealed a material difference in what the evidence could support.

items.prompt: How would you explain a complex policy to both specialists and the general public?
items.modelAnswer: I would preserve the same evidence and central reasoning but change the route into the subject. Specialists would need assumptions, technical definitions and uncertainty ranges. A general audience would need the practical consequences, clear explanations of key terms and examples that illuminate rather than replace the evidence.

items.prompt: What is the difference between accessibility and oversimplification?
items.modelAnswer: Accessibility removes barriers that prevent an audience from understanding a point; oversimplification removes distinctions that are necessary to understand it accurately. An accessible explanation can use plain language while retaining qualifications, uncertainty and the limits of the evidence.

items.prompt: How does register affect the relationship between speaker and audience?
items.modelAnswer: Register signals formality, expertise, distance and sometimes institutional authority. A highly formal register may suit a regulatory notice but create distance in a community meeting. A more direct style can build rapport, provided it remains respectful and appropriate to the stakes.

items.prompt: Why should the evidential standard remain stable across audience versions?
items.modelAnswer: If the speaker changes the evidential standard to secure agreement, adaptation becomes manipulation. Different audiences may need different explanations, but the claims, qualifications and uncertainty should remain faithful to the underlying evidence. Otherwise the versions no longer communicate the same analysis.

items.prompt: Give an example of framing that is useful but transparent.
items.modelAnswer: A speaker might frame a transport proposal around access to jobs because that is a central public concern, while acknowledging that cost, noise and distributional effects also matter. The frame helps listeners see relevance without pretending that it exhausts the issue.

items.prompt: How can a speaker establish shared assumptions without excluding dissenters?
items.modelAnswer: I would identify premises that are genuinely common, such as the need for reliable services, and avoid claiming consensus on disputed values or methods. Where assumptions are uncertain, I would state them explicitly and invite scrutiny rather than treating them as universal.

items.prompt: What risks arise when a public message relies heavily on emotional appeal?
items.modelAnswer: Emotion can make consequences vivid, but it may crowd out uncertainty or encourage audiences to infer more than the evidence supports. A responsible appeal connects human relevance to verifiable information and avoids presenting a compelling example as representative proof.

items.prompt: How would you adapt a technical term for a non-specialist audience?
items.modelAnswer: I would give a concise definition, explain why it matters to the decision and use an example that preserves the important distinction. I would retain the technical term where the audience may encounter it later, but not assume that naming it is the same as explaining it.

items.prompt: Should the same message always be delivered in the same tone?
items.modelAnswer: No. Tone should reflect the setting, audience expectations and purpose. A crisis update may require directness and calm; a consultation may call for openness and acknowledgement of uncertainty. The factual content should remain consistent even as the interpersonal approach changes.

items.prompt: How can you tell whether an adapted explanation has remained faithful?
items.modelAnswer: I would compare the claims, evidence, assumptions and qualifications across versions. If the accessible version implies greater certainty, omits a material limitation or changes the scope of the conclusion, it is no longer a faithful adaptation. Feedback from the intended audience can also reveal whether the explanation is clear.

content.audioTranscript: The communications team prepared two versions of the same research briefing. The specialist version retained technical terminology, detailed assumptions and uncertainty ranges. The public version used local examples and maps to explain the practical implications. The team emphasised that the projections were scenarios rather than guarantees. Although the wording differed, the evidence and limitations remained the same. The project lead argued that this was audience adaptation, not simplification at the expense of accuracy. The purpose was to help each group understand the decision without concealing what the model could not establish.
